title: Japan strikes back at the B-29s
pull: The last pilot drew a pistol

facts.text: Three days after B-29s from the Marianas bombed Tokyo for the first time, on 24 November 1944, the Imperial Japanese Navy struck back at the bombers' home, Isley Field on Saipan.

Early on the morning of 27 November, two twin engine Betty bombers from Iwo Jima came in low. They caught Superfortresses being loaded with bombs for the second Tokyo mission, destroyed one B-29 and damaged eleven.
At noon came a second strike: Zero fighters of the 252nd Air Group, each carrying a bomb, guided toward Saipan by two Myrt reconnaissance planes. Historic Wings describes it as a one way mission.
They flew low over the sea to stay under the American radar. One Zero clipped a wave with its propeller, dropped its bomb and was shot down by Thunderbolts near Pagan.
The rest slipped through and swept over Isley and Kobler fields with complete surprise. They destroyed three B-29s and badly damaged two more.

The defenders shot the raiders down one by one: AAF fighters got four and antiaircraft gunners six. In the confusion the gunners also shot down an American P-47, a loss the official report called "inexcusable".

The last Japanese pilot, out of ammunition, landed his Zero on Isley Field and opened fire on the Americans with his pistol until infantry rifle fire killed him. Brigadier General Haywood Hansell, commander of XXI Bomber Command, saw it happen.
The raids went on into January. In all, the Japanese sent more than eighty planes over Saipan and Tinian, destroyed 11 B-29s and damaged 43, and killed 45 Americans, but lost about 37 aircraft.
The raids came from Iwo Jima. After 27 November, Admiral Nimitz ordered a heavy strike on the island, and the bombing of Iwo Jima went on until the Marines landed there on 19 February 1945.

photoNote: Tier: green. A parked B-29 in the foreground with another Superfortress burning behind it, black smoke filling the sky, Saipan. Album caption: "Superfortress is burning in background, showing the proximity of the parked planes, after Jap air raid on Saipan, 11/27/44." U.S. Air Force photo 55506AC, NARA 342-FH-3A40451 (naId 204976767), public domain. Cropped from the scanned album page (labels and border removed), saved 1833 x 1398. Scale and drama rather than faces; no photo of the Japanese airmen exists in the public domain. Runner up: "Burning Boeing B-29 in revetment", 27 November 1944, 342-FH-3A40459 (naId 204976781), saved as photos/1944-11-27-saipan-raid-b.jpg. Also strong but not dated on its caption: engineers ram a bulldozer into a burning B-29 after a low level attack, 342-FH-3A40427 (naId 204976713, caption on the back of the page; received 16 Dec 1944, so it could be 27 Nov or 7 Dec).
photoCredit: A B-29 burns behind a parked Superfortress after the Japanese raid on Saipan, 27 November 1944. U.S. Air Force photo, NARA 342-FH-3A40451, public domain.

declassified.fact: Nimitz's answer came on 8 December 1944: P-38s, B-29s and B-24s dropped 814 tons of bombs on Iwo Jima, and three heavy cruisers fired 1,500 eight inch and 5,334 five inch shells at the island.

film.record: 111-CB-35, Combat Bulletin No. 35, "Japs Raid Saipan B-29 Base" story (NARA 24321)
film.shot_notes: Uploaded by another helper (R2 copy checked with media.py exists). Times on the full bulletin: 00:00 to 00:33 Combat Bulletin and Signal Corps titles; 00:34 to 00:39 title card "Japs Raid Saipan B-29 Base" and 00:40 to 00:47 map (avoid both). 00:48 to 00:53 night antiaircraft fire, tracer dots; 00:54 to 01:11 explosions and fires at night, big flare ups at 00:56 to 00:58 and 01:02 to 01:10 (best opening: fire on the airfield at 00:56); 01:12 to 01:20 burning wreckage at first light; 01:21 to 01:45 a bulldozer and men fighting the fires; 01:46 to 01:55 black smoke over the tent lines; 01:56 to 02:17 a burning B-29, fire crews with hoses 02:00 to 02:05, the wrecked tail 02:10 to 02:17. 02:18 starts the next story (blood plasma). The track has sound (mean level about minus 22 dB): a Combat Bulletin soundtrack, almost certainly narration with music, not period sound; listen before keeping it, or run the clip silent. Sound set false by the research run: the Combat Bulletin soundtrack is narration, so the clip runs silent unless a listen proves a natural sound stretch.
film.license: Public domain, U.S. government work (U.S. Army Signal Corps / War Department, NARA Record Group 111).
film.date_note: Combat Bulletin 35 does not date the raid on screen; the Film Library calendar ties this story to 27 Nov 1944, and the fires and bulldozer work match the Air Force photos dated that day. The night stretch could include the predawn Betty attack; if unsure, caption it as the Japanese raids on Isley Field, November 1944.
